Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible

📅 2026-11-05 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Industry observers note that I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs. More about Eric ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career. Now I want to share this knowledge with you.

Accessibility is a core part of a functional digital experience. As the LLM chat pattern continues to spread like wildfire across the web, we risk excluding people if these experiences are not built with accessibility as a core consideration.

It is also worth re-mentioning what “exclusion” means here: It’s the loss of knowledge, the loss of opportunity, the loss of utility, the loss of employability, the loss of entertainment, and more.

“Immersive LLM chat experience” is a catch-all term for full-screen experiences like Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, America.gov, Glean, and other similar websites and web apps:.

Industry observers note that the majority of what this post covers applies to both web apps and native apps. This is because these experiences are typically built using web technologies, then placed in a native wrapper via frameworks such as Electron or Tauri.

Immersive LLM chat experiences are not patterns such as a pop-up chat, inline text generation utilities, or summarization tools. These simpler applications of LLM technology will have different considerations and expectations. Instead, this is a starting point for making those other experiences accessible.

There is nothing special about chat-based UIs when viewed via the lens of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. They are interactive experiences, built using web technologies. The losses I’ve described — and the legal liability associated with them — are access barriers in the same way any other web content can be an access barrier.

I would also like to mention the social model of disability here: the idea that exclusion can be created by the built environment. For example, consider an elevated entryway that uses a gently sloping ramp in place of stairs.

It has been revealed that built environments also extend to digital experiences, and the social model also applies here. The main activities undertaken to operate an LLM chat are already well-established:.

It is how we facilitate — or fail to facilitate — those interactions that’s the salient bit.

Before we get into the technical aspects, we must consider the overwhelming visual bias that permeates software creation.

We live in a highly visual culture, so our outputs unconsciously reflect and reinforce that. What we need to do here is be aware of and think through the non-visual considerations.

While not all disabilities are blindness or low vision conditions, a lot of the core interactions of an LLM chat do need specific accommodations for these two types of disability.

Recall the social model of disability here, and how it applies to the main flow of using an LLM-based chat. You:.

Let’s demonstrate at a high level what someone who can fully see the screen experiences compared to someone who uses a screen reader and cannot see the entire screen, or large portions of it:.

Visually, we can see the LLM reply appear. Someone who uses a screen reader does not know new content has appeared because:.

So, how do we create an experience for someone who uses a screen reader that is equivalent to the experience of someone who can fully see the screen? To start, we use live regions.

According to recent reports, live region announcements will enable someone to know what the LLM has responded with without having to move focus from the input used for prompting. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, glancing upwards to read the LLM response when it appears.

In a recent development, first, read this excellent article by TetraLogical if this is your first attempt at getting live region announcements working. They’re tricky to get right, and this article sets the record straight.

One common pitfall I want to call specific attention to is applying aria-live on each LLM response message. Don’t do this. Instead, use a dedicated live region area to announce each message’s content.

The live region area should be placed at the end of the DOM and used for all live region messaging. This method is far more stable and reliable, which is important for ensuring everyone understands what the experience is communicating.

With that established: What we want to do is trigger a live region announcement when the LLM’s chat reply shows up in full on the screen.

This creates an outcome where you can read the message if you can see the screen, and hear or feel the message if you cannot.

Industry observers note that there are a few things to do when creating a good user experience for the people who rely on these live region announcements. These considerations mean the difference between a compliant-yet-unusable outcome and something that genuinely works for the person using it.

Attempting to announce the message as it streams in may create a juddering and confusing experience that’s difficult for someone to parse.

It is better to wait until the message has completed streaming, and then announce the message’s content in full.

Responses from an LLM often take time to complete. Generally speaking, there are three ways to show a response is still processing:.

Industry observers note that these experiences are typically only shown visually. If you cannot see the screen, it may lead to it feeling like the experience has stalled or crashed — especially if the response is for a large or complicated request that takes a while to work through.

To address this, we’ll want to use live region announcements:.

Industry observers note that if text is visually shown on the screen: Ensure a companion live region announcement is also triggered at the same time the loading message text is displayed. The text string for the live region announcement should be the same as what is shown visually, to be sure to ensure parity of experience:.

If a text-less loading animation is shown on the screen: Ensure the loading state is also communicated to assistive technology.

According to recent reports, A live region announcement that mentions the reply is loading after a set amount of time will facilitate an equivalent experience for this interaction. It doesn’t have to be too verbose; the word “Loading” can suffice:.

Triggering the loading message five seconds after prompt submission seems to be the sweet spot, according to the inclusive user research I evaluated. You can then have your logic repeat the loading message every five seconds until the LLM completes its actual reply.

Be sure to also announce the reply immediately as it finishes streaming. You don’t need to wait until the next five-second loading message cycle is complete.

Recent findings suggest that also consider randomly selecting from a set of different phrases that communicate that a response is being formulated after the initial “Loading” message is dispatched. This helps in scenarios where someone may think the loading experience itself has crashed or stalled.

In a recent development, we’ll eventually be able to replace the technique TetraLogical outlined with ariaNotify(). It is a much-needed and welcome addition to the platform, and will drastically lower the hacks and headaches many developers encounter when creating and managing live region announcements.

Recent findings suggest that baseline lists the ariaNotify() method as having cross-browser availability at the time of this article’s publication. However, there are two factors to consider here:.

Also consider that while a polyfill for ariaNotify() is available, you need to factor in whether it has both:.

What this realistically means is holding off for a while on ariaNotify() in favor of the tried and true TetraLogical live region technique.

Industry observers note that headings are the most popular way people who use screen readers navigate around an experience. Because of this, I advocate for inserting visually-hidden headings before each chat message.

Here’s a simplified version of that in code:.

And here’s what the code might look like using the actual content from a human question and an LLM response:.

So, why the “You remarked:”/”Cody said:” prefix? Remember the visual bias. Visually, we can see the left- or right-hand alignment of messages, used to indicate who is saying what.

Industry observers note that the prefix serves the same purpose: identifying the message’s owner. This allows people to quickly move through a conversation the same way someone might quickly scroll upwards to re-establish context, checking who said what and when.

Sources indicate that using landmark regions to wrap the larger overall areas of your LLM chat experience helps people understand its overall layout. It can also enable quick screen reader navigation to each area:.

Sources indicate that landmarks allow someone who cannot see the screen to learn about its overall makeup. This is the equivalent of how we rapidly move our eyes and tilt our heads to different overall areas when scanning the screen to initially learn the overall layout of an experience.

Recent findings suggest that I am hesitant to wrap chat messages in section or other landmark elements. The reason for this is that they “pollute” the list of landmarks a screen reader can generate, making navigation more laborious. This is especially relevant for long-running sessions where many messages are present.

Compare the following and ask yourself which one would be easier to move through with your keyboard if trying to jump from the prompt content area back to the sessions area:.

Here, our visually hidden heading elements serve as a dedicated navigation mechanism for moving through the LLM conversation.

In addition to headings and landmarks, there are two other ways to let people get around promptly:.

Skip links — sometimes referred to as skip navigation — allow you to rapidly jump to another area on the same page or view.

Sources indicate that skip to main content links are commonplace on many mature websites and web apps. Immersive LLM chat experiences should be no different.

Place a skip link in the DOM that allows someone to jump to the main conversation area before any other DOM content that is shown visually on the screen.

Also consider using additional skip links that enable:.

In a recent development, composite widgets are used when a discrete section of content contains multiple interactive elements. Focus is then managed within this section by the developer, so that:.

In a recent development, for the purposes of an immersive LLM chat experience, we want to make conversation lists composite widgets. This enables someone to swiftly navigate both within and past the entire list.

It has been revealed that here, consider the use case of someone who exclusively relies on a keyboard to navigate. Compare pressing Tab 50 times to get through each of the 50 conversation sessions you’ve created versus pressing Tab once. Now consider motor control conditions where those keypresses can be fatiguing, or even painful to perform.

Once someone places focus on a conversation list composite widget, they can use the Up and Down arrow keys to navigate through each conversation session list item.

As a quality-of-life improvement, I also like to support the following keyboard interactions:.

To save you a lot of headaches and prototyping: Corner cases around focus management and usability expectations for people who rely exclusively on keyboards work against you if you try to go with a feed pattern approach.

There’s no need to unnecessarily overcomplicate things. The article elements’ wrapping messages with visually-hidden headings approach that I’ve described earlier is both simple and effective.

It has been revealed that people who use assistive technology understand the simpler approach, and it involves far less effort to maintain. It’s a win-win!

Industry observers note that pressing F6/Shift+F6 to hop around different areas of the app is an older navigation technique some people who use Windows screen readers employ when navigating through installable desktop apps. Think of it a lot like navigating by landmark.

LLM chat experiences are effectively apps in their own right. Because of this, we can recreate the F6 navigation experience and accommodate those who might attempt it. That means:.

According to recent reports, there’s no secret sauce here. For starters, place an id on each landmark, as well as tabindex="-1". Also ensure each landmark other than main has an accessible name, granted via either aria-label or aria-labelledby.

After that, have an event listener set up to recognize Control+F6 and Control+Shift+F6 key presses. Set focus to:.

And voilà! We now have web-based F6 navigation.

As it is an older technique, people who are younger or less experienced with screen readers may not know F6 navigation exists.

Consider socializing the capability in the accessibility portion of your application’s settings menu to address this lack of awareness. Also consider exposing and making F6 navigation re-bindable as another discovery technique, provided your application supports keyboard shortcut rebinding.

According to recent reports, again, this advice only applies to an immersive LLM chat experience. Help agent popups and other less-sophisticated experiences have different expectations.

There are two areas that deserve more finesse when considering where to set focus when F6 navigation is used: the prompting input and the conversation.

Setting focus directly on the input used to type prompts — and not its parent form landmark element — allows someone to quickly get into the action.

Similarly, setting focus on the visually hidden heading of the last message displayed allows them to rapidly jump to the content the LLM generated — a data attribute such as data-last-message can be really helpful for managing this.

It has been revealed that using F6 and Shift+F6 keypresses allows someone to hop from the chat input to what the LLM outputs, then back again. This enables rapid keyboard-based review and iteration on an LLM’s output.

Adjust the text size of your experience and double-check that content is not clipped, or that there’s horizontal overflow.

It has been revealed that people increase the text size of the experiences they use, and more than you’d probably guess. They also resize application windows. Also consider that most LLM-based chat designs tend to use a smaller text size to allow for more information shown on screen.

Because of these two factors, it makes sense to evaluate how your experience holds up when the browser font size is increased.

Sources indicate that customization lives at the heart of accessibility. It’s only natural that LLM-based chat experiences have preferences to better accommodate all the different ways people use them.

In that vein, thoughtful preference offerings can go a long way to helping out people with access needs. Here are some that I’ve found to be particularly useful.

Industry observers note that some LLMs perform interim actions that are circumstantially less notable than the messages they ultimately generate. Here, consider programming-oriented LLMs. They can perform actions like researching and reasoning, code search, and tool calls.

These secondary actions typically have a smaller, less visually vital treatment compared to the messages that contain the main LLM response content. This is because the results are more important than the methodology when using this type of interaction.

Announcing each of these secondary actions could lead to a confusing or overwhelming experience, especially if multiple actions are clustered and fire off live messages in rapid succession.

To address this, you can allow people to circumstantially switch off the announcements for this type of ancillary information. The content in the conversation is still present; it just isn’t announced via a live region. This is equivalent to how someone who can see the screen can skim over them.

Letting someone re-enable these types of announcements also grants parity in experience, in that it allows them to know the actions are happening if they want a more information-intensive experience. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, intentionally paying close attention to the LLM’s actions.

It has been revealed that it might also be worth investigating letting people toggle visually hiding and showing these less key announcements, as well. This can help people with attention or cognitive considerations, who may be less familiar with technical jargon.

Loading animations and large animated effects, like streaming conversations and side panels expanding and collapsing, can be distracting for some people with attention and cognitive considerations. That can go a long way toward breaking someone’s flow.

To address this, you can provide a toggle to turn off animations, reducing their transition time to zero.

You should also strive to be a respectful and courteous steward of the experience. Default your animation toggle to an off state if a request for a reduced motion experience has been in the device operating system. You can use the prefers-reduced-motion media feature to achieve this. Also consider a setting that can re-enable animation, even if a reduced motion request is present.

Some people can get distracted by, or have their focus disrupted by, sound effects. This is similar to animation considerations.

Letting people turn off app-specific sound effects means they don’t have to mute their entire device. Here, consider things like other apps playing flow state-inducing music or white noise that they might be using to help them focus.

Alternatives for sound-based notifications include, but are not limited to:.

I am of the school of thought that any experience that uses keyboard shortcuts also needs to allow both editing and being switched off, both in bulk and on a shortcut-by-shortcut basis.

You may be quick to think of conflicts with assistive technology, but I’d also like to take this space to remind you of different language keyboard layouts.

Live region messages are plain text strings. These strings are announced by screen readers in full in one go from start to end.

Semantic information that comes for free by using the appropriate HTML element isn’t present in live region announcements—it’s stripped out. Because of that, we need to think about how we could make our live region content both clear and useful.

Recent findings suggest that each type of special content has its own considerations. For my work, I created special cases for tables and blocks of code:.

A table’s cell content will sound odd when declared without the companion semantic structure conferred by elements such as table, th, tr, and td. Relationships between columns and rows aren’t present in a live region announcement, either.

Because of this, we can convert the live region announcement of tables to use a concise description of the number of rows and columns, plus a general description and overall trends it might highlight.

A block of code sounds like gibberish when the line breaks are stripped away, and the content is flattened into a single string.

And if it’s a large block of code, it can be a tedious amount of gibberish to parse — nobody wants to sit through an announcement of 2,376 lines of code, painstakingly declared character-by-character.

To accommodate this, we can convert the live region announcement of code blocks to use the filename or file type, plus how many lines of code the block contains.

Industry observers note that also note here that people can revisit the actual message content itself. The actual message content will ideally have the appropriate semantics applied to it. This means things like tables being unveiled as, and navigated through as, table content.

In this way, the live region message is a context-setting preview of what to expect. This is the equivalent of rapidly visually skimming a message as it is streaming in, then scrolling back to review its content with more attention afterward.

All of the previous is built atop feedback from testing different approaches and noting what works, and what could be improved. You want to facilitate disabled people being the experts in their own lived experience, and not treat others’ advice as the more credible source.

Inclusive user research is a vital way of determining if an experience is actually usable. Centering disabled people’s observations and perspectives is a way to take an experience beyond baseline compliance and create something usable and equitable.

According to recent reports, it is vital to ensure that everyone can use chat-based LLM interactions as the pattern continues to proliferate. Although this is not an exhaustive list of everything you’ll need to do, the content above covers a wide swath of the main places accessibility barriers and friction may show up.

It is my sincerest hope that the improvements I’ve learned about and implemented can help you with your efforts to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who use assistive technology to get what they want or need online.

Thank you to Sarah Higley, whose research and efforts in this area informed key parts of this work.

"All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the upcoming Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.
  • The beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes.
  • It has been revealed that ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the newly introduced Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the upcoming Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

The beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

It has been revealed that ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the newly introduced Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks.

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

In a recent development, that last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

It has been revealed that in our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the big deal.

Industry observers note that A both bigger and smaller matter is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Recent findings suggest that that is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

Sources indicate that the architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

In recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same challenges that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

According to recent reports, to be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility complications – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many owners, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Hunters Point Library.

According to recent reports, the solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers.

Sources indicate that that leaves only a deeper concern, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings, both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do – leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once remarked, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

Recent findings suggest that as is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

  • It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum demonstrates today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

With The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh indicates, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused Latest Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the challenges that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

“I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”.

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is presently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she indicates has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she noted.

The Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Industry observers note that muholi was born in 1972 in Umlazi, Durban, South Africa and lives today in Cape Town. They are a self-described visual activist, who, since the mid-2000s, have used photography to document the lives of LGBTQ+ people, initially in South Africa, where they were born.

Zanele Muholi, Diana Cristina Nascimento Ramos, Salvador, 2025, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

They have since expanded their project around the world and work in discrete, often ongoing series that have a common aim: to respond to violence and discrimination against queer and trans communities, to reflect their defiance and resistance, and to expand their visibility in visual culture in South Africa in particular but also far beyond.

In a recent development, zanele Muholi, Ashara Ekundayo, Venice, 2026, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

Sources indicate that the people they depict have, since the start, been far more than sitters or subjects; they are collaborators, participants who help define the way they are represented. A crucial factor is that Muholi turns the lens onto themself. “When I position myself in my own frame,” they have noted. “I do so on my own terms attempting to articulate my own way of seeing and wanting to be seen.”.

Industry observers note that zanele Muholi, Christine Madonsela, Daveyton, Gauteng, 2017, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

And whether it is their unflinching and tender portraits of their collaborators or their imaginative and improvised self-portraits Muholi’s photographs are always beautiful objects, with a fastidious attention to the properties and possibilities of their medium.

In a recent development, zanele Muholi, Mantedieng ‘Mantis’ Mamabolo-Cunningham, Parktown, Johannesburg, 2018, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

In a recent development, they discuss the influence of their mother, who was a maker herself, and was a profound influence on one of their most notable works, Somnyama Ngonyama (2012). They reflect on the enormous impact of photographers including Rotimi Fani-Kayode, Lola Flash and Joan E. Biren, writers including Audre Lorde, and musicians including Brenda Fassie. Plus, they answer our usual questions, giving insight into their daily practices and the rhythms of their work, and reflecting on the ultimate question: what is art for?

This podcast is sponsored by Bloomberg Connects, the arts and culture platform.

Bloomberg Connects offers access to a vast range of international cultural organisations through a single click, with upcoming guides being added regularly. They includeseveral guides to institutions that have shown and collected Zanele Muholi’s work, including SFMOMA in San Francisco, Tate in the UK, the Center for Visual Arts in Denver in the US, and MEP, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie in Paris. On the guide to the MEP, you will find features on its current exhibitions. They include Penn and Fashion, exploring the photographer Irving Penn’s long association with the fashion world, in which his stripped-back style has had a lasting influence on generations of photographers. You can hear audio features on all the sections of the exhibition, from his early years at Vogue magazine in the 1940s to the photographs made when Penn was in his 90s of Karl Lagerfeld, John Galliano and Christian Lacroix. You can also explore the related exhibition in La Petite Galerie, called Everyday Clothing, which allows young visitors and families to explore the creative process through works from the MEP’s collections.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.

The 20×20 series, launched to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a big impact on the next 20.

With just 10 years between the start of their practices, Escobedo and Lanza Atelier represent two crests on a upcoming wave of Mexican architecture that has brought regional references to the world stage and made adventurous but sympathetic interventions at home in Mexico City.

Escobedo was one of Lanza Atelier’s Alessandro Arienzo’s teachers at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and he and partner Isabel Abascal cite her as an inspiration whose success with kindred ideas has given them the confidence to pursue their vision.

They are becoming known for distilling complexity down to simple and pure gestures, whether in the appropriately snaking crinkle-crankle walls of their Serpentine Pavilion, inspired by the English countryside, their Cancun house with materials and forms drawn from sea snail shells, their Re-Source exhibition design that visitors could take home, or their hierarchy-challenging Family of 4 chairs, prompted by the arrival of their second son.

For Escobedo’s part, she identifies Arienzo and Abascal’s dedication to concept and process, which involves extensive research and testing, as key to their strength.

“Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous,” noted Escobedo. “They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play that makes their architecture both thoughtful and joyful.”.

The Lanza story began in 2015, with toilets. Arienzo was approached by a client who, nearing the end of their bike path development in Mexico City, realised that they needed public bathroom facilities along the route. Arienzo suggested to Abascal, originally from Madrid, that they work on together on the project.

Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous. They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play.

Promptly, their collaboration turned one of architecture’s humblest structures into a nexus for meaning and care.

“We were exploring the scarcity of means and materials, but also the boundaries between inside and outside, and how to make something very simple like a toilet become something larger, like a meeting point and a resting space,” said Abascal.

“And also how to initiative for the future of public architecture that might not be very taken care of or maintained by combining landscape and construction.”.

The finished project features semi-open structures built from concrete blocks and filled with planting, creating a network of shaded resting points along the exposed track.

In a recent development, from the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza. Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since].

Bamboo trees loosely divide the male and female toilets, but they share common sinks – a feature that Lanza Atelier pushed for as part of their vision for a space of respectful coexistence between all customers.

“It came out really naturally and fun, and simple,” said Arienzo. “That first interaction made Lanza happen because we needed to build a tech giant after that.”.

The nature of the collaboration pushed them to establish a distinct language from the get-go, adds Abascal.

“From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza,” she said.

It has been revealed that “Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]. We explored so many different options, and we were so opinionated about how it should be. We very rigorously really gave all the importance to designing a toilet.”.

As Escobedo identifies, Lanza Atelier’s work has a remarkable sense of play considering it lacks the colour, ornamentation or usual curlicues that would prompt association with the word.

Their use of materials is almost austere, in the sense that many of their projects have seen them hone in on just one material and push it to its limits, as in the local Sienna bricks of their Serpentine Pavilion.

Recent findings suggest that arienzo characterises this “extreme” approach as being “maybe a phase” more than a signature of the studio’s work. Instead, the key feature is how they arrive at the choice.

In a recent development, “We pick materials because of where the project is or what we have close to the site,” Arienzo mentioned. “We analyse what’s the best or least aggressive way to build [in that place], because, we always say, building is really violent.”.

Using fewer materials also allows them to focus more on questions of space, and makes it easier for their pavilions and installations, often demountable as a matter of principle, to find a second life.

“The main glitch is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract,” said Abascal.

The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract.

That’s where the playfulness comes in, the designers identify, allowing them to dig into various elements, flip them, manipulate them and be curious about them.

“That, I think, is the playground,” adds Arienzo.

When asked what qualities each of the duo brings to the table that makes their work together so strong, Arienzo is initially flippant.

“I’m the bad cop,” he states with a smile.

But when the duo finally answers seriously, their responses do seem to reveal something about the alchemy going on behind the scenes.

Industry observers note that “I used to call Alessandro’s gaze towards the world ‘the laser eye’,” said Abascal. “He is always pointing things out to me – mostly in our everyday lives, it’s things that the city creates and produces informally, but his laser eye applies to every context.”.

“And it’s not only something visual but has to do with how things are and are put together and solved.”.

For his part, Arienzo describes Abascal as the powerhouse behind Lanza’s ideas and concepts.

“I think she gives a lot of meaning to the projects,” said Arienzo. “I think without this, I would just do soulless stuff. She connects the work with history, with literature, with art.”.

In a recent development, lanza Atelier’s slate currently includes a house in LA to replace one destroyed by the wildfires, several projects in Mexico City and the design for the Expanded Tradition exhibition on contemporary Mexican craft at Qatari museum M7. When we speak, Abascal is on her way to the Canary Islands to conduct research on their architecture for migrant pregnant mothers. It’s a patchwork that is idiosyncratically Lanza.

Neither Arienzo or Abascal seems to be the type to have a 10-year plan – asked about professional goals, Arienzo replies that they’re more orientated towards taking better care of themselves and their children – but they identify housing, particularly collective housing, as the type of architecture they most want to work on.

They hope to do it within a global industry that demolishes less and values what’s already built more, and that learns from the original “sustainable architecture” of vernacular construction in places like Mexico.

The country has been in the spotlight in the last few years as one of the few in Latin America with a progressive government, and one whose president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has frequently had to stand her ground against its northern neighbour.

Asked about whether government policy has had any positive effect on architecture and related industries at home, Abascal and Arienzo’s good cop and bad cop come out.

“From architects of the older generation, our generation and the younger generation, I can feel a sense of optimism,” remarked Abascal.

“I feel a sense of doing nothing,” said Arienzo. “Claudia is way better than what there was before; I’m a leftie. But I think there should be many more competitions around housing in the city.”.

Both say they would like to see more public competitions in place of private developments, and that they would eagerly enter.

It has been revealed that “Mexico City’s downtown is beautiful and it’s almost empty,” mentioned Arienzo. “There isn’t a lot of density. I think it should be much more about that. Housing is a substantial glitch and will be forever for these big cities.”.

Sources indicate that there is an ideal future for the architects, then. It’s one that would see the urban landscape of their home city benefit from the respect, creativity and serene beauty that is the Lanza calling card.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

Industry observers note that A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

According to recent reports, the critical distinction is probate. In states with expensive or slow probate processes — California, New York, Florida, and many others — a living trust pays for itself many times over. In states with simplified probate procedures (like Texas or Wisconsin for small estates), the cost advantage of a trust is smaller but the privacy and incapacity benefits still apply.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:.

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

Recent findings suggest that for most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, Fresh Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate initiative.

Industry observers note that the remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:.

A will alone is likely sufficient if:.

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:.

Add irrevocable trust structures if:.

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Recent findings suggest that the most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate strategy.

In a recent development, yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate blueprint should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific challenges or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

In a recent development, A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

In a recent development, the living trust vs will decision is not about which is better — it is about which is better for your specific situation. For estates with more than $100,000 in probatable assets, especially in high-cost probate states, a revocable living trust saves thousands of dollars and months of delay while providing incapacity protection and privacy that a will cannot match. For smaller estates in simplified-probate states, a well-drafted will with proper beneficiary designations may be all you need. Either way, the worst estate plan is no estate plan. More than 60% of American adults have neither a will nor a trust, leaving their families to navigate probate without guidance, pay avoidable costs, and endure unnecessary delays during the most difficult time of their lives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JKR rebuilds KFC around its bucket in the KFC Bucketverse: custom type, a redrawn Colonel, and a bucket that frames everything.

The move is simple and hard to argue with. Instead of inventing a latest symbol, JKR took the one object every KFC customer already knows and made it the system. The bucket is now a frame: it holds food photography, illustration and campaign lines, and it scales from a cup to a building. The logo itself turns three dimensional, the Colonel gets a warmer expression and a collar under his bow tie, and the red, white and black palette stays exactly where it was. Nothing about the brand gets thrown out. Everything gets pointed at the bucket.

According to recent reports, two custom typefaces carry the voice. Kentucky Fried Serif and Kentucky Fried Sans were drawn with StudioDRAMA, and the serif does the heavy lifting: it spells KFC at poster scale on the bucket, the bag and the building, with thick strokes and tight spacing that read from across a street. The stripes, once a background pattern, are reworked into a type-based asset that carries its own messages, and the boxes repeat lines like BIG KFC FLAVOR DIALED UP TO 11 and NOTHING HITS LIKE KFC ORIGINAL CHICKEN in stacked red caps. Tobias Hall drew the Finger Lickin' Good lettering, which now works as a mark in its own right, set in script against the block serif.

It has been revealed that the system holds together because the same decisions repeat at every size. The kraft bag carries the serif wordmark at full height. The restaurant facade draws the bucket outline across the whole frontage in white line on red, with the Colonel sitting above the door. Inside, curved screens run giant red letterforms behind the counter, and the KWENCH drinks range gets its own vertical sign. A global roster of illustrators adds the colour: Bernardo Henning's loose, bright drawing fills the back of a black T-shirt, and a silver bucket pendant turns the packaging into jewellery. The photography follows the same rule, shot from inside the bucket looking up, so the food and the people sit inside the frame the brand built.

See more from JKR on their website.

Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

It has been revealed that A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

Rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

Sources indicate that every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

An AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

We can call that the break-even line. Returns to owners come in three forms:.

Industry observers note that for example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool demonstrates the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

Industry observers note that four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

Recent findings suggest that these questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

Run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the issue alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

Sources indicate that count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom says to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

You can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

According to recent reports, who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

According to recent reports, A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

Industry observers note that compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

Industry observers note that for example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

According to recent reports, the nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

Industry observers note that every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

It has been revealed that error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

It has been revealed that automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, people stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

Map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

Show owners where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

According to recent reports, letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

It has been revealed that still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

Research in radiology reveals how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result indicated how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

Question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

Ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

Sources indicate that table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

Industry observers note that put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

Let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

Question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

Question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

Question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

On Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

Industry observers note that question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

According to recent reports, A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

Sources indicate that the feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

Sources indicate that two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

Everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that newly introduced capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

In a recent development, audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

Start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that owners might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

The attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

💡 Key Takeaways
