Comment | A missed opportunity for a full accounting of cultural cleansing

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is always gratifying to see one’s work referenced—especially 20 years after the fact.
  • According to recent reports, the vast exhibition spans art, digital re-creations, photography and filmed interviews.
  • Recent findings suggest that A wall text references my 2006 book The Destruction of Memory: Architecture at War, which first set out systematically why such targeting happens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is always gratifying to see one’s work referenced—especially 20 years after the fact. The exhibition Heritage in Resistance: Timbuktu to Odessa, at the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine in Paris (until 3 January 2027), traces attacks on material and intangible culture in conflicts beginning with the dynamiting of the Bamiyan Buddhas in 2001 and ending in Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza.

According to recent reports, the vast exhibition spans art, digital re-creations, photography and filmed interviews. It is conceived of as an investigative report organised into sections on erasure, resistance and repair.

Recent findings suggest that A wall text references my 2006 book The Destruction of Memory: Architecture at War, which first set out systematically why such targeting happens. The exhibition credits me with coining the term “cultural cleansing” in respect of the Bosnian War to explain the pattern of heritage erasure that can accompany, or presage, ethnic cleansing and the persecution of populations. It notes that Unesco adopted the term from 2012 to describe “the destruction of World Heritage Sites by terrorist groups”.

Except that book notes much more than that. It talked about this same process in other places such as the Israel-occupied West Bank. It examined cultural genocide (like cultural cleansing, this still has no definition in international law) witnessed in instances ranging from the Ottoman Empire and Native American populations to the Holocaust and Tibet. I would now add the experiences of the Uyghurs in China, the Rohingya in Myanmar, the Yazidis in Iraq and the Palestinians in Gaza to that dreadful list. I argue that patterns of heritage destruction can evidence genocidal intent. Other genocides, such as that in Rwanda, did not have a pronounced material culture component.

These are matters that the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine exhibition unacceptably skirts. As in Germany and the UK (where a talk at London’s Building Centre including Architects for Gaza was cancelled following an intervention by Lawyers for Israel this summer), the French state and its institutions are censoring pro-Palestinian voices.The crucial work of Forensic Architecture in documenting destruction, for example, is not present after a dispute over the group’s use of “the G word”. How can you explain what has happened to Gaza’s cultural heritage unless you are at least prepared to discuss possible intent and patterns of destruction?

As an investigative report, the show obfuscates as much as it reveals. Institutions and governments shield themselves behind the argument that it is up to the courts to determine genocide. They forget the Genocide Convention’s duties of prevention—as litigated in the 2007 International Court of Justice (ICJ) case, Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro, or South Africa’s inclusion of attacks on culture when considering Palestinian “conditions of life” at the ICJ.

An installation view of Heritage in Resistance: Timbuktu to Odessa, at the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine in Paris, until 3 January 2027 Photo: © Didier Plowy.

There is an impression that heritage destruction in conflicts has got worse over recent decades and that the propaganda impact of destruction is actually exploited by some groups. The jury is out on this. As reflected in the show, however, the international heritage community has had an almost singular focus on actions by terrorist groups, whereas over the past decades (Islamic State and its affiliates aside) it has been the firepower of United Nations State Parties that has been overwhelmingly responsible for the devastation to material history—including but not limited to the United States, Russia, China, Israel and Saudi Arabia. Isis iconoclastically wrecked religious sites in Mosul, but it was the liberating forces that comprehensively flattened the historic city.

Looting, too, is problematically covered in the Paris exhibition. This is a serious issue in war zones where security vanishes. But the myth repeated here that the sale of looted artefacts is a meaningful source of terrorist funding “on a par” with resources such as oil is simply unevidenced. (Recovered Isis documents show something quite different.).

The exhibition is sponsored in part by the French office of Unesco. No surprise then that the organisation’s manifest failure to protect heritage in conflicts is absent from the walls. Unesco is celebrated—as it should be in some cases—for its work in Timbuktu, where the International Criminal Court brought the first (and, to date, only) successful prosecution for the targeting of monuments as a war crime. Less convincingly, the show argues that this episode was a turning point after which Unesco formulated a more grassroots approach to preserving culture by working with local people on local priorities.

It was Unesco that disgracefully praised Putin for liberating Palmyra despite the terrible damage Russian forces allied with Assad inflicted on Syria’s people and heritage. Unesco has been just as partial since: while it “strongly condemns” Russian attacks on heritage in Ukraine and Israel’s on Lebanon, it does not offer the same degree of pressure in its statements on heritage destruction in Gaza or Iran. Even then, unlike other UN agencies, Unesco never names Israel. Unesco has not invoked the 1954 Hague Convention in relation to Gaza, despite citing it in virtually all similar instances. Unesco did not seek urgent action by the UN Security Council or the General Assembly to protect cultural sites there as it did in respect of Isis.

The Paris show is more subtle in its understanding of the ways that post-war heritage reconstruction can be problematic and not necessarily healing, but is just as silent on Unesco’s move away from the centrality of authenticity to reconstruction work. Whereas the notion of rebuilding the Bamiyan Buddhas was deemed unacceptable, Unesco promoted building a brand-upcoming Mostar Bridge in Bosnia and Herzegovina as peacebuilding—despite community relations actually deteriorating in the city. And then the agency had the temerity to declare the facsimile bridge a World Heritage Site, undermining its own scientific tenets to bolster a failed symbolic gesture. All this bad-faith is set out in my follow-up book, Monumental Lies (2022).

Sources indicate that one is left to read between the lines for hints at the full curatorial mindset. Once through the exhibition doors, the first large-scale works displayed are photographs by the Palestinian artist Taysir Batniji of Gazans’ retrieved housekeys, with their heartbreakingly quotidian fobs—a friendship bracelet, a cheap carabiner clip, a Minnie Mouse figure. The unknown fate of their owners is pencilled in below.

It has been revealed that in its silences and voids, Heritage in Resistance at least accurately mirrors failures of international institutions and laws and the partiality and misinformation that surrounds responses to contemporary heritage destruction. Ultimately, the show offers false hope about successful resistance via digital surveying, reconstruction and Unesco work. What we should be feeling is despair.

But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

New York Times Prohibits Photographers From Using Photoshop 2027

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest version of Adobe Photoshop, Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0), added many AI-powered photo-editing features.
  • As The Verge reports, The New York Times sent an email to freelance photographers and contributors warning them against using Adobe Photoshop 2027.
  • The email, which was shared on social media, specifically cites features inside Photoshop that use generative AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest version of Adobe Photoshop, Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0), added many AI-powered photo-editing features. Not all photographers are thrilled about the increasingly heavy focus on generative AI inside Photoshop, and photojournalists are taking note, too.

As The Verge reports, The New York Times sent an email to freelance photographers and contributors warning them against using Adobe Photoshop 2027.

The email, which was shared on social media, specifically cites features inside Photoshop that use generative AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.”.

The Times‘ worries about Photoshop 28.0.0 are more about a perceived lack of clarity surrounding the application’s photo-editing features than the presence of AI itself. Photoshop has included generative AI in many tools for years, including Generative Remove and Generative Expand. The latest release uses generative AI for even more tasks, such as relighting and restyling photos.

Fresh York Times photojournalists and freelance contributors cannot use generative AI on their photos. In fact, as the publication’s ethics standards outline, all published photos must be accurate depictions of real events. This means no people or objects can be added, rearranged, blurred, distorted, or removed. It also means that cropping must be done carefully so as not to omit any relevant details in a scene. Color can be adjusted, but only minimally and in service of accurately reproducing an event as it happened.

The Times adds that any use of AI, including generative AI, must be clearly disclosed to readers. The organization has long embraced Adobe’s C2PA initiative as it relates to image provenance and metadata, and that is not changing.

What has changed, apparently, is how easy it is for a photographer to inadvertently use a feature inside Adobe Photoshop that relies on generative AI, which will then show up in the metadata. This appears to be the primary concern for The Latest York Times, as it cannot work with photos that are labeled as AI-edited content.

According to recent reports, “It has come to our attention that certain functions in Adobe Photoshop 2027 utilize generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to users of the software. At this time we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using this new version when working on assignment for The Times,” New York Times spokesperson Graham James tells PetaPixel.

To prevent these challenges, all contributing photographers must entirely avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignments for The Times—an unprecedented blow to Photoshop’s already wavering reputation among professional photographers. Fortunately, it is possible for customers to install previous versions of Photoshop through the Creative Cloud app, although it’s not necessarily straightforward. As of this writing, users can roll back to Photoshop 27.0, but no earlier.

Adobe’s insistence on publicizing its generative AI features, rather than the genuinely good and mostly inoffensive improvements made earlier this month to Adobe Camera Raw and Lightroom, has created quite a stir in the photography community. The Times‘s upcoming policy will certainly not help Adobe’s PR problem with photographers.

PetaPixel reached out to Adobe for comment but did not hear back ahead of publication. This story will be updated with any response.

"Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.
  • Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for new designs: the finds from archaeological digs.
  • However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.

Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for new designs: the finds from archaeological digs.

However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.

Deselected finds are duplicates, common in type, poorly preserved or otherwise judged to have limited future research value.

“The material that you see here is the lowest of the lowest quality,” said Isarin at a preview of Ex Situ at this year’s Dutch Design Week. “It’s not preserved. It doesn’t belong in a museum. It doesn’t belong in a depot.”.

In fact, if it is not going to be used for educational purposes or reference collections, deselected archaeological finds are required by Dutch law to be carefully destroyed, as they are in many places around the world, noted Isarin and Klaster.

Although the materials may be of low value to archaeology, the designers both found this something of a waste. With Ex Situ, they aim to explore a new category of use and preservation for these materials, believing artists and designers have the capacity to tell stories of heritage in a different way to museums.

With the permission of the province of South Holland, they gave deselected materials to nine Dutch practitioners with expertise in crafts such as ceramics, woodwork and glassmaking.

One of the most finished pieces, exhibited in a preview showcase at October’s Dutch Design Week in the Klokgebouw, was by footwear designer and materials researcher Judith Sanders.

In a recent development, she crafted the foundation posts from a section of the Roman Limes border road, dated to 125AD and built under the emperor Hadrian, into the heel of a pair of high-heeled shoes. Sanders was intrigued by the notion that they could perform structurally once again – this time bearing the load of just one person.

Bold numbers on the sides of the shoe denote where on the dig site the material came from, while a second pair of shoes works leather from the middle ages into a modern-day sneaker silhouette.

Another piece is by designer-maker Daan Simons, who worked with 14th-century wood fragments from a ship that was wrecked and then subsequently used in the construction of Rotterdam.

The texture and existing peg holes in the wood are preserved in his Remembrance Pots, which he imagines holding the ashes of a loved one or a keepsake of theirs, compounding the layers of memory in the vessel.

Klaster and Isarin started on the path to Ex Situ after meeting accidentally at their timber drying kiln, where she was having some wood dried for a furniture project, and he was having the deselected Roman posts dried in the hope they would find another life.

Recent findings suggest that “Intrigued by their blackness”, Klaster asked Isarin if she could have them, and went on to make a series of tall vases. That was five years ago, and they have been discussing the potential intersection of archaeology and design ever since.

Klaster says that the Ex Situ designers were supported with information about heritage and the finds they were working with, but that the project naturally inspired some trepidation.

“In the work that they have made so far, you see that they have thought it through, and there is respect in what they made,” stated Klaster. “But the first cut with a scissor or a bandsaw is, of course, a scary thing.”.

Industry observers note that “[One of the designers] was like, can I really saw that in two? And I said yes, you can. If you have a proposal as a designer, yes, it’s yours.”.

That worry will be echoed among some archaeologists, Isarin adds, and he and Klaster’s aim is for the exhibition to promote discussion among the profession.

Recent findings suggest that “For archaeologists, this material is in a sense sacred,” said Isarin. “But it’s deselected, so nobody wants it.”.

Sources indicate that he said that while reactions have so far been positive, the concern becomes more thorny if the design were to take place in a commercial context – for instance, if Sanders’ shoes were sold by a fashion brand. In that sense, some archaeologists may see this project as opening a Pandora’s box.

“As soon as we enter the commercial world, then I think for many archaeologists it will be, even though it’s deselected material, an interesting debate ethically,” stated Isarin.

According to recent reports, “Suppose that all this matter, which has no value at all, that somebody gets rich out of it. That would be a disaster for many archaeologists.”.

Nevertheless, Klaster and Isarin think it is a debate worth having.

Pieces in the exhibition come from practitioners ranging from glass artist Bernard Heesen, working with 17th- and 18th-century glass, to conceptual material designer Shahar Livne, working with mammoth bone, and ceramicist Lotte Douwes, working with Roman pottery.

“We have so much rich material beneath our feet, with amazing stories from 40,000 years up to today,” noted Klaster.

The exhibition was previewed at Dutch Design Week, alongside the maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive installation by Maison the Faux and Boris Acket and design collective Show Not Show’s Table of Power exhibition.

Ex Situ: Matter in Translation will be on at See Lab, The Hague, from 5 February to 7 March 2027, with discussion events as part of its programming. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

#150029. Industry News: An archaeological take on ancient rituals in the heart of a legendary Berlin nightclub

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (959 w)

Industry News: An archaeological take on ancient rituals in the heart of a legendary Berlin nightclub

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “The world is changed.
  • Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, an artist duo hailing from Iran and Canada, respectively, expertly blended archaeology, artificial intelligence (AI), acoustics, chemistry and sculpture to create a profoundly multi-sensory experience in A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads earlier this autumn (2-18 October).
  • Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, Sūryasya Śántau (Within the Solar Silence), 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “The world is changed. I feel it in the water. I feel it in the earth. I smell it in the air. Much that once was is lost, for none now live who remember it.” Cate Blanchett, as the high elf Galadriel, spoke these opening lines in The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), and in darkened cinemas around the world, her delivery set the tone for the wonder that followed. Not since my first viewing of that film 25 years ago had I felt that sense of being dwarfed by mythology, and to re-experience it in Berlin’s famous nightclub Berghain of all places was a delight.

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, an artist duo hailing from Iran and Canada, respectively, expertly blended archaeology, artificial intelligence (AI), acoustics, chemistry and sculpture to create a profoundly multi-sensory experience in A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads earlier this autumn (2-18 October).

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, Sūryasya Śántau (Within the Solar Silence), 2026. Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe.

It has been revealed that situated inside Halle am Berghain—a gargantuan former power station that, yes, was reminiscent of J.R.R. Tolkien’s Khazad-dûm—the installation was presented by the Berlin-based contemporary art initiative House, helmed by Juliet Kothe, who co-curated with Nadim Samman. The exhibition was co-presented by the Autotelic Foundation, whose whimsical take on AI art in Venice had been one of the standout digital presentations during the most recent Biennale.

It has been revealed that at the centre of A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads was a towering, eight-minute-long, 4K video installation that slowly panned through a digitally rendered, 4,000-year-old Mithraic cave temple, created based on 3D scans of the ancient site. Originally made for an exhibition in Lausanne in 2025, the installation was expanded to take advantage of the Halle am Berghain’s size.

According to recent reports, as the “camera” floated through the ancient temple in the looping video, visitors were encouraged to position themselves in the center of the installation, where they would be encircled by human-height black monolithic speakers. Each speaker featured a different voice, all chanting in an AI-generated, speculative Proto-Indo-Iranian (PII). PII is the ancestor of the Indo-Aryan and Iranian language families, including Sanskrit and Avestan. There are no historic documents or written texts in PII, let alone documented Mithraic chants from that period.

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, A Shroud Woven of Solar Threads, 2026. Installation view, Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe.

Recent findings suggest that to realise the vital sonic component of the installation, the artists worked with the University of Toronto, drawing on comparative linguistics to reconstruct plausible linguistic forms. AI then allowed them to bring the speculative language to life. One of the speakers, Roushan remarked, was based on her own mother’s voice, which had been used to train one of the AI chanters.

It has been revealed that "Mithra…" the chant began, referring to the ancient solar deity, a kind of lesser-known Ra, and as the incense burning in the hall filled one’s nostrils it was difficult not to feel transported by the sheer scale and the acoustic prowess of the installation. Near the ceiling, graffiti of the Eye of Horus that pre-dated the exhibition oddly contributed to the compounding of ritualistic symbols that have accumulated in the hall.

It has been revealed that ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, To Have a Shell is to Surrender, 2026. Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe.

It has been revealed that there is an inherent futility in worshipping an ancient sun god for any kind of wish-fulfillment. But ritualistic production and devotion have persisted through millennia and in our lives today, be it in our fascination with our illuminated, hand-held screens, or our commitment to attend public dance events that encourage abandon—such as the one that took place the weekend of Roushan and Stankievech’s opening, several metres and a few layers of concrete away. Objects scattered throughout the exhibition space included replicas of Bronze Age bells and reliefs, objects of ritual and religious significance that adorned the space and further contextualised the spiritual dimension of the installation, although none so potent as the ever-burning incense.

Industry observers note that “We are all subject to digital change in society, economy, politics,” Nadim Samman, the Autotelic Foundation’s director, says. “These changes are massive, they are abrupt and they are intense. Making sense of it needs to come from below. Artists offer crucial ways to understand what this change means. Without artists, we are just stuck with the narratives and the images supplied by the companies that make the technology. Digital change impacts culture, and artists can help us understand what that impact actually feels like, and how we can think it through.".

In a recent development, ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, The Most Naked Thing in Existence, 2026. Halle am Berghain Courtesy of HOUSE in partnership with Autotelic Foundation. Photo: Noshe.

Since we have no recordings of PII, it is hard to refute that AI contributed a vital component of the installation. The exhibition’s thoughtful and archaeological approach to incorporating technologies that help us to speculate on the past was a welcome counterpoint to many digital art exhibitions in recent memory.

Roushan and Stankievech’s ambitious undertaking stands as one of the highlights of what has been a busy year for digital and AI-generated artistic presentations. The rather romantic gesture of leveraging AI to take us back several thousand years, to a time of fascination with nature and solar worship, and the decision to do so within the Brutalist context of a power-station-cum-nightclub, cleverly brought together many disparate threads.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The images were taken by the spacecraft’s Visible and Infrared Observation System camera, developed by Northern Arizona University, at around 9 A.M.
  • Recent findings suggest that the images were captured by the second of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft to perform a powered flyby of Earth this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA’s ESCAPADE spacecraft has captured an incredible photo of the Earth as it slingshotted past the planet on its way to Mars.

The images were taken by the spacecraft’s Visible and Infrared Observation System camera, developed by Northern Arizona University, at around 9 A.M. EST on November 9. This was approximately three hours after the spacecraft made its closest approach to Earth, when it was about 38,500 miles away and had a clear view of the Western Hemisphere.

Recent findings suggest that the images were captured by the second of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft to perform a powered flyby of Earth this month. Both spacecraft used a combination of engine burns and Earth’s gravity to gain momentum for their 10-month journey to Mars.

Once they reach orbit around the Red Planet, the spacecraft will study how the solar wind — a stream of charged particles traveling at around a million miles per hour from the Sun — interacts with Mars’ environment and contributes to the loss of its atmosphere.

A commercial satellite captured images of the pair from approximately 3,000 miles away, while a member of the mission team photographed the spacecraft passing overhead from his home near Los Angeles (below).

Two spacecraft. Two flybys. One path to Mars.

Photographed from the Los Angeles area, Blue and Gold streaked through the same part of the sky two days apart—Blue in blue, Gold in gold. https://t.co/9SDOMmqqtY.

— Rocket Lab (@RocketLab) November 23, 2026.

NASA explains that the ESCAPADE mission is funded by NASA’s Heliophysics Division and is part of the agency’s Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration program. The University of California, Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory leads the mission, working with partners including Rocket Lab, NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Advanced Space, and Blue Origin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roboto Studio rebuilt the Flowhub brand identity around one mark, Helvetica Now and Neon Moss green, from the website to the checkout screen.

Flowhub runs point of sale, payments, ecommerce, marketing and reporting for specialty retailers across the United States, from cannabis dispensaries to liquor stores and CBD shops. More than $4B in sales passes through it every year. Its old purple identity is gone. In its place, Roboto Studio built a system on a single mark, one typeface and one bright green, then carried the same parts into the website and the product interface, so the homepage, the dashboard and the payment screen at the counter are made from the same pieces. The line that runs through it all states it plainly: Retail moves fast. We move faster.

Helvetica Now does the talking. Display Bold carries the headlines at sizes that fill the frame, white on Rich Black, while Display Medium, Text Medium and Text Regular step down through the interface without changing voice. The specimen page lines the weights up beside a full character set, and the restraint demonstrates in how little else the layouts need. The mark is a compact flowing form that reads at a glance and crops into a poster motif at bus stop scale. On the homepage the grid keeps real product screens in view, a strip of retailer logos leading into the hardware and apps, Maui OS, ecommerce, kiosk and delivery, each shown as the actual screen.

Recent findings suggest that two materials carry the system. Liquid chrome gives the mark its weight, a molten rendering that turns up on the poster, the SOC 2 shield and the map of backers. Frosted glass does the quieter work, layering the interface panels, the one platform stack and the deal cards Max drafts over photography. Color stays disciplined. Pearly White and Rich Black cover most of every surface, Pearl holds the panels, Neon Moss appears only on the one action that matters, and Sunburst orange is kept for anything that needs attention. The Intelligence dashboard opens on what needs attention today, sales, margin and stock value at the top, with Max drafting a reorder before a bestseller runs out. At the counter, the payment screen turns fully Neon Moss with a single word, Paid, large enough to read from the customer side.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production company Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

In a recent development, to do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a big part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”.

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he said.

“His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between demonstrates across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and Upcoming Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

“That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time highlights were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he noted.

“We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”.

It has been revealed that J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent demonstrates at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Other set designs recently featured on Dezeen include Dave’s London show, which Stufish illuminated with a laser-shooting piano.

Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

📅 03 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry.
  • The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience.
  • For many, tattoos are much more than art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

In a recent development, psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos demonstrated no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It notes, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

According to recent reports, in a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings highlighted that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

It has been revealed that apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, has been out in the wild for a month now, and more apps are being updated to natively support the dual-screened device all the time. Adobe Lightroom just got a massive iPhone Duo compatibility revision this week, and it is a strong example of how good the Duo can be.

As Adobe Photoshop and Lightroom Product Designer, Johannes Eckert, explains on Threads, the Adobe team has worked hard to fully optimize Lightroom for Duo.

The iPhone Duo version of Lightroom works as normal on the device’s front screen, but when opened up, it is an entirely transformed experience, showing photos much larger than on other iPhone models and moving editing tools to the side. There’s also a “laptop pose,” as Eckert says, that puts editing tools on the bottom while the photo stays above the fold.

Recent findings suggest that in PetaPixel‘s testing, the updated app worked as promised and delivered a genuinely pleasant mobile photo editing experience. It’s nice to see my photos on the Duo’s large internal screen and to be able to access sliders, presets, masking tools, and more without obscuring my photo at all or needing to shrink it way down. You can still actually see your photo while utilizing Lightroom’s suite of editing tools, which is a big improvement over a standard iPhone photo editing experience.

That remarked, there is still some room for improvement, and it seems like Adobe is already working on making tweaks. For example, when doing a Curves edit, the curves themselves appear on as an overlay on the photo, which is fine, except that it leaves much of the Duo’s inner screen totally empty.

“I think it’s better to have the curves to [the] right to get rid of the empty space,” Threads user itsrongarcia commented on Eckert’s original post.

“We agree. This will be in the next update!” Eckert replied.

Other customers are looking forward to Adobe bringing some of its more powerful editing tools over from iPad, arguing that Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip is more than capable of running things like automatic dust removal and AI-powered noise reduction. There’s no word yet on whether Adobe is considering these things at this time.

Adobe will no doubt refine the iPhone Duo version of Lightroom further as more real-world consumers get to test it out and offer their feedback, but so far, so good. Ultimately, the iPhone Duo’s lasting appeal will depend heavily on how apps utilize its distinct form factor. Lightroom is definitely taking full advantage of it, and Lightroom mobile has never been as enjoyable to use.

#150021. Museums finding fresh ways to measure wellness initiatives’ value

Museums finding fresh ways to measure wellness initiatives’ value

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that museum programming in the US has been branching out recently, much of it in the direction of connecting art to health and wellbeing.
  • Sources indicate that the qualitative data from a caregiver's perspective does not necessarily include the point-of-view of the person struggling with cognitive decline.
  • Sources indicate that the Frye is at the forefront of art and health initiatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that museum programming in the US has been branching out recently, much of it in the direction of connecting art to health and wellbeing. As part of this trend, institutions have been creating programmes for people living with memory loss. But these present unique challenges, particularly when it comes to evaluating their success.

Sources indicate that the qualitative data from a caregiver's perspective does not necessarily include the point-of-view of the person struggling with cognitive decline. This is why institutions like Seattle’s Frye Art Museum try to do a lot of in-the-moment observations and feedback rather than relying exclusively on formal surveys.

Sources indicate that the Frye is at the forefront of art and health initiatives. Each quarter, the museum offers a special programme for medical residents, students and teaching professionals from nearby hospitals, designed to develop perspective-taking and empathy. Meanwhile the museum recently expanded its Creative Aging initiative, gallery-based experiences and hands-on artmaking in partnership with the University of Washington's Memory and Brain Wellness Center.

Located in Seattle’s First Hill neighbourhood and surrounded by medical centres and senior living facilities, the Frye has served older adults experiencing memory loss for 17 years. Its Creative Aging programme began with a former employee’s experience caring for her mother with dementia, and has since expanded to reach broader communities of older adults.

Sources indicate that the Frye's experience in the field highlights a broader challenge facing museums as arts-and-health programming expands. The Lancet medical journal recently published a call for translating growing evidence of the arts’ health benefits into more equitable access, stronger healthcare partnerships and research into how programmes work in practice. For museums, a big question is how to evaluate these initiatives while responding to community needs.

Participants at one of the Frye’s Creative Aging programmes Photo: Runyon Colie, courtesy the Frye Art Museum, Seattle.

Sources indicate that susan Magsamen, the founder and executive director of the International Arts + Mind Lab at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, sees this kind of programming as an opportunity for museums to expand their public roles. She describes art as “a superpower that we have forgotten” and museums as institutions that contribute to “human thriving and flourishing”.

It has been revealed that magsamen compares the growing integration of health and wellbeing into museum missions with the emergence of education as a core museum function in previous decades. “Beyond things like attendance, revenue and membership, we need to think about a scorecard,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “What is the institutional performance and public benefits?”.

The Frye has been using the Art Bridges Foundation’s Art + Wellness Toolkit, which includes validated measures across four areas of wellbeing: social, emotional, cognitive and physical. The museum is right now evaluating four programmes, incorporating the toolkit's terminology into its materials and developing surveys using its standardised measures.

“This common language has been valuable as we grow programmes under art and wellbeing," states Lea Lovelace, the Frye’s associate director of creative aging programmes.

Jill Sonke, a co-author of the Lancet study, underscores the importance of measuring behavior and patterns of engagement, so that the most vulnerable can access the arts and their underlying health benefits. “Institutions need to also measure who’s not coming,” she states, “why they don’t see themselves in the programming.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the quickly developing field, Sonke cautions museum staff to move ahead carefully. Enthusiasm for evidence can create its own problems. If institutions set out primarily to prove that their programmes work, evaluation instruments can inadvertently be designed to confirm the outcome they hope to find. “We need to make sure that we’re designing objective, open measures that will allow us to really understand the experiences of the people we’re seeking to serve,” she notes.

One of the Frye’s Creative Aging programmes Photo: Runyon Colie, courtesy the Frye Art Museum, Seattle.

Sonke also questions whether additional assessment is always warranted: “If the evidence exists already, if it’s not really necessary, then it’s not ethical to put people through the burden of assessment.".

According to recent reports, the Frye has experienced these tensions firsthand. "It's a balancing act," claims Tamar Benzikry, the museum’s director of learning and engagement. "We are careful about 'survey fatigue', because we realise you might not get the information requested because our audience is burnt out from surveys.".

Sonke, despite her caution, underscores the importance of “making relationships and normalising the idea that museums should be talking to public health folks, and public health folks should absolutely be talking to museums”.

The Frye is always working with community leaders to identify barriers to participation and create programmes that strengthen connections between the museum, public health and healthcare. The team looks to share experiences at a convening of museum professionals next May, while incorporating arts and health more deeply into its 2027 exhibition programme.

Activities will include gallery-based creative movement inspired by works of art and led by a physician who is also a trained dancer. There are also looks for folklore-inspired slow-looking and storytelling sessions led by a professional storyteller with training in gerontology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new photography book offers a glimpse into Europe’s underground rave culture at the turn of the millennium, documenting the free-party movement through the eyes of two photographers who were part of the scene.

Sources indicate that never Alone 1997–2004: Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, features 160 original analog photographs made between 1997 and 2004. The images document a period when free parties were spreading across Europe, offering an alternative to mainstream society through music, community, and a shared rejection of conventional lifestyles.

Rather than documenting the movement as outsiders, Clementi and Morandi were active participants in the culture. Their photographs provide a firsthand account of a counterculture built around emotion, affection, and togetherness, at a time when music and personal connections — rather than social media and mass communication — brought people together.

According to recent reports, the book spans 196 black-and-white pages and brings together previously unseen photographs that capture the atmosphere and values of the era. Its accompanying text is written by Tobia D’Onofrio, author of Rave New World, who explores the history and significance of the European free-party movement.

“Rave was born as a disappearing ritual in which the art of invisibility was practiced, and parties were temporarily autonomous and free zones that appeared and disappeared into thin air within a few hours,” says D’Onofrio.

According to recent reports, “1997–2004 can therefore be considered the golden age of the so-called illegal free parties and of rave culture. It was the moment of the phenomenon’s expansion across Europe… the rave scene had been criminalized to the point that in 1994 the Criminal Justice Act in England outlawed free parties. At that point, the energies shifted to the rest of Europe, and Italy immediately became the scene of legendary parties.”.

The book examines how rave culture developed into more than a musical movement. It represented a rejection of conventional working and social structures, embracing communal living, constant movement, and a different relationship with time and space. Free parties became meeting places for people united by anarchic sensibilities and a desire to escape everyday routines.

Clementi and Morandi both attended the same high school in Milan before pursuing separate careers. Despite taking different paths, both remained dedicated to photography, eventually bringing their shared rave-scene experiences together in Never Alone.

The book is available online and through specialist bookstores.

RIBA president rejoins ARB register to restore architect title

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework at the moment only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a new regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson said his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

According to recent reports, “Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”.

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he stated he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

It also proposes upcoming legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

“I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

“While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”.

Williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

Tech Report: European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.
  • Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal.
  • European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins claims about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins notes about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins notes this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins states you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in latest people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Industry observers note that coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins claims, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.
